templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
No punctuation inside a compound joined by and
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
Dash pair around a supplementary element
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a participial opener
items.passage: At Hamoukar, an ancient city in northeastern Syria that was destroyed by fire around 3500 BCE, excavators have uncovered collapsed mudbrick fortifications and more than a thousand small clay ______ the size, shape, and placement of these objects, the excavation team concluded that they were projectiles hurled from slings during a siege.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “more than a thousand small clay balls.” The second sentence opens with the participial phrase “Studying the size, shape, and placement of these objects,” which describes its subject, “the excavation team,” and then gives the main verb “concluded.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma lets “studying the size, shape, and placement of these objects” describe the excavators in the first clause, so the main clause “the excavation team concluded that they were projectiles hurled from slings during a siege” is then joined to the main clause “excavators have uncovered ...” with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, “small clay balls studying the size, shape, and placement” attaches the phrase to the first clause, and the main clause “the excavation team concluded ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “And” tries to pair “studying ...” with “have uncovered,” which is not parallel, and the main clause “the excavation team concluded ...” is still joined to the first main clause with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Hamoukar, northeastern Syria: a city destroyed by attack and fire around 3500 BCE; excavations in the 2000s found collapsed walls and more than a thousand clay sling bullets). Known facts, no names. Band-6 shape of b15724fc and 1b97cce9 (participial opener of 10 words with its own series commas); the comma version reads at first as a participle on “excavators,” and the splice appears at “the excavation team concluded,” 12 words after the blank. One-sentence run of 52 words.

band7.why: S1_period with a 10-word gerund-participle opener carrying its own series commas; the splice shows 12 words after the blank. Gerund and prepositional openers are the band-6 kind (band7 section 3.3), as planned.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a long past-participle opener with its own series
items.passage: Between 1937 and 1939, archaeologists at Begram, in present-day Afghanistan, excavated two storerooms that had been walled up nearly two thousand years ______ with ivory carvings from India, painted glassware from the Roman world, and lacquered bowls from China, the rooms may have held a royal treasury rather than a merchant’s inventory.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “walled up nearly two thousand years earlier.” The second sentence opens with the participial phrase “Packed with ivory carvings from India, painted glassware from the Roman world, and lacquered bowls from China,” which describes its subject, “the rooms,” and then gives the main verb “may have held.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma makes “packed with ivory carvings ...” describe the storerooms in the first sentence, so the main clause “the rooms may have held a royal treasury ...” is joined to the main clause “archaeologists at Begram ... excavated two storerooms ...” with only a comma, a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “two thousand years earlier packed with ivory carvings ...” keeps the phrase in the first sentence, and the main clause “the rooms may have held ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “And” pairs “packed with ...” with “had been walled up,” so the phrase becomes part of the clause about the storerooms, and the main clause “the rooms may have held ...” is still joined to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (the Begram hoard, Afghanistan: in 1937 to 1939 French archaeologists opened two walled-up rooms holding Indian ivories, Roman glass and Chinese lacquer; whether it was a royal treasury of the Kushan period or a merchant’s stock is debated, hence “may have held”). Known facts, no names. Band-7 checks (band7/boundaries.md section 6): opener of 21 words with internal series commas, attachable to clause 1’s last noun phrase; cue outside a 6-word window (splice at “the rooms may have held,” 21 words after the blank); run 50 words; reasoning steps 3. Differs from b3’s past-participle item by the series inside the opener and the and-coordination decoy.
band7_moves: opener of 21 words, a past participle with its own three-part series that reads naturally as a description of clause 1’s storerooms (storerooms that had been walled up ... earlier, packed with ...)
“and packed” coordinates smoothly with “had been walled up,” so the comma, glued and and options all hold until the splice at “the rooms may have held,” 21 words after the blank

band7.why: 21-word past-participle opener with internal series commas that hangs naturally on "storerooms" in the comma reading; splice revealed at "the rooms may have held", far outside a 6-word window; and-coordination decoy is attractive. Matches a872c60a and 0fa289a7.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing the first clause: “though” before a semicolon
items.passage: In 1997, a genetic analysis classified Xenoturbella, a simple wormlike creature inhabiting seafloor sediments off Sweden, among the mollusks, the group that includes clams and snails. The animal is not a mollusk at ______ the molluscan DNA in that analysis turned out to have come from bivalves it had eaten.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The adverb “though” belongs to the first clause: the claim that “The animal is not a mollusk at all” contrasts with the previous sentence, in which a genetic analysis classified Xenoturbella “among the mollusks.” A comma sets “though” off from that clause, and a semicolon joins it to the next main clause, “the molluscan DNA in that analysis turned out to have come from bivalves it had eaten,” which explains the correction.

B.recipe: semicolon with a non-clause; logic-wrong adverb placement
B.why_wrong: Placing “though” after the semicolon turns what follows into a dependent clause, and a semicolon cannot join a main clause to a dependent clause. It would also present the source of the DNA as a contrast with the claim it explains.

C.why_wrong: Commas on both sides of “though” leave the two main clauses, “The animal is not a mollusk at all” and “the molluscan DNA in that analysis turned out to have come from bivalves it had eaten,” joined by only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no mark after “though,” the word becomes a conjunction that presents the bivalve DNA as a concession, as if its source were at odds with the claim that the animal is not a mollusk. The source of the DNA is the reason for that claim, so the contrast belongs with the previous sentence instead.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Xenoturbella, a simple marine animal from Swedish seafloor mud; a 1997 DNA study grouped it with mollusks, and later work showed the mollusk DNA came from bivalves it had eaten; it is now placed far from mollusks). Known facts, no names. Band-7 checks: logic-wrong distractors B and D, decided by the previous sentence (cue outside a 6-word window); run 25 words, like 790fc366 and 21e58a83; reasoning steps 4.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1, which corrects the previous sentence (placed among the mollusks vs not a mollusk at all)
clause 2 explains clause 1 with the same polarity, so the textbook placement (; though) and the subordinator reading (, though) fail only on meaning (logic-wrong B and D)

band7.why: Option set of 790fc366 and f78997cf: ", though;" key closing a clause that corrects the previous sentence; "; though" and ", though" fail only against meaning and the earlier sentence (two logic-wrong distractors), ", though," splices.

review.note: D (", though" with no mark) is grammatical only as a subordinating "though", which makes the eaten-bivalve DNA a concession to the claim it explains. CB offers the identical ", though" shape as a wrong option in f78997cf and rejects it as an unmarked boundary between main clauses; this item adds the meaning reason. Kept.

safety.unfair: D reads 'though' as a subordinating conjunction ('at all, though the molluscan DNA ... turned out'): grammatical, only the concessive logic is off
safety.lead_override: 2026-10-27 lead: safety listed D ', though' (conjunction) as defensible. D makes the DNA-source clause a concession, but that clause is the reason the animal is not a mollusk, so D fails on meaning; key A ', though;' is CB's band-7 S1_adverb shape (f78997cf). Same call as w4b1_04 and w4b5_04.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause: semicolon before “rather”
items.passage: Observing in 1990 that far less capital flows from wealthy countries to poorer ones than standard economic models predict, economist Robert Lucas did not reject the models’ underlying ______ he argued that differences in workers’ skills and education diminish the returns that capital can earn in poorer countries.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “economist Robert Lucas did not reject the models’ underlying logic” and “he argued that differences in workers’ skills and education diminish the returns that capital can earn in poorer countries” are both main clauses. The adverb “rather” introduces the second clause as the alternative to what Lucas did not do, so a semicolon joins the clauses before “rather,” and a comma sets the adverb off from the clause it opens.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the main clauses “economist Robert Lucas did not reject the models’ underlying logic” and “he argued that ...” run together, a fused sentence.

B.why_wrong: Commas around “rather” are not enough to join the two main clauses; without a semicolon or period before “rather,” the result is a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the main clauses “economist Robert Lucas did not reject the models’ underlying logic” and “he argued that ...,” a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: social science, economics (the Lucas paradox: in a 1990 paper Robert Lucas asked why so little capital flows from rich to poor countries and pointed to differences in human capital, among other factors). Known, real; the passage stays at the paper’s core claim. Band-6 shape and menu of a9e5b788 (3.5: novel / novel, / novel; rather, / novel, rather,): rather opens clause 2 after a not-clause, a shape band 7 never uses. One-sentence run of 48 words, the context folded into an introductory participial phrase.

band7.why: "; rather," opening clause 2 after a not-clause is the band-5/6 adverb shape (band 7 never uses rather); menu of a9e5b788, long participial opener lengthens the run.

review.note: Fame call: the Lucas paradox is known inside economics courses but is not textbook or pop-science famous for SAT students (not on the order of Braess), and a Boundaries item cannot be answered from background knowledge; kept. The attribution is Lucas's real 1990 argument (human capital differences narrow the predicted return gap).

items.subtype: No punctuation in a restrictive title plus names
items.passage: In 1994, researchers sampling a frigid spring on Disko Island, Greenland, discovered a microscopic animal with complex jaws made of tiny interlocking parts. In 2000, Danish ______ and Peter Funch formally described the species as Limnognathia maerski and assigned it to a new group, Micrognathozoa.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Danish zoologists” is a title that comes directly before the names it describes, “Reinhardt Kristensen and Peter Funch,” with no article in front of it, so the names are essential to the subject and take no punctuation. The subject, “Danish zoologists Reinhardt Kristensen and Peter Funch,” then leads straight into its verb, “formally described.”

A.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate the title “Danish zoologists” from the names that complete it, and nothing closes the element the comma would open.

B.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete main clause; “In 2000, Danish zoologists” is not one, so the colon breaks up the subject.

C.why_wrong: The comma separates the two names joined by “and,” “Reinhardt Kristensen” and “Peter Funch,” which together form the subject of “described.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Limnognathia maerski, a microscopic jawed animal found in 1994 in a cold spring on Disko Island, Greenland, and described in 2000 by Reinhardt Kristensen and Peter Funch as the first member of Micrognathozoa). Known, real names. Band-6 shape of d4fe8f03 (plural title before two names joined by and) and 4dcedc31 (title + name as subject). Menu: key, comma after the title, colon after the title, comma after the first name.

band7.why: Plural title plus two names joined by and as the subject (d4fe8f03 shape); local decision, distractors plausible.

items.subtype: No punctuation in a restrictive title plus name, followed by a verb in an embedded clause
items.passage: Hatena arenicola, a single-celled organism inhabiting Japanese beach sand, harbors a green alga. When it divides, only one daughter cell inherits the alga; the other develops a feeding apparatus and must capture a replacement, a pattern that ______ may resemble an early stage in how certain algae acquired chloroplasts.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The title “biologist” comes directly before the name it describes, with no article in front of it, so the name “Noriko Okamoto” is essential and is not set off by commas. No punctuation is needed between the subject, “biologist Noriko Okamoto,” and its verb, “suggests,” or between “suggests” and what she suggests, that the pattern “may resemble an early stage.”

A.why_wrong: The commas treat “Noriko Okamoto” as extra information, but the name is essential: without it, “biologist” has no article and does not identify anyone.

C.why_wrong: The comma after “Okamoto” separates the subject from its verb, “suggests,” and the comma after “suggests” separates the verb from what she suggests.

D.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate the title “biologist” from the name that completes it.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Hatena arenicola, a flagellate from Japanese beach sand described in 2005 by Noriko Okamoto and Isao Inouye; at division one daughter keeps the green algal symbiont and the other, colorless, develops a feeding apparatus; the authors proposed it as a secondary symbiosis in progress, an early stage of the way some algae gained their plastids). Real, known names. Band-7 checks: S4_restrictive is local at every band (section 6 exempts it from the window check); second slot after the name; run 39 words.
band7_moves: title + name sits inside a relative clause (a pattern that biologist Noriko Okamoto suggests may ...), and a second slot follows the name: the verb plus the clause it introduces, as in 0a114526
commas around the name look polite (A), and the comma after the name (C) looks like closing a parenthetical

band7.why: Title plus name embedded in a "that ... suggests may" relative clause, with the second slot after the name (comma before and after "suggests") as in 0a114526; commas around the name look polite. As hard as the band-7 S4_restrictive officials, which are local at every band.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase that holds a relative clause
items.passage: More than four thousand years ago, the Egyptian official Harkhuf returned from Yam, a distant region south of Egypt, with ebony and incense. The young king Pepi II, however, was preoccupied with something ______ dancer whom the king, in a letter Harkhuf afterward had inscribed on his tomb, urged him to guard day and night.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The young king Pepi II, however, was preoccupied with something else” is a complete main clause that announces what occupied the king. A colon correctly introduces the noun phrase that names it, “a dancer whom the king, in a letter Harkhuf afterward had inscribed on his tomb, urged him to guard day and night.” That phrase is not a clause: “urged” belongs to the relative clause beginning with “whom.”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “a dancer whom the king ... urged him to guard day and night” is a noun phrase; its only verb, “urged,” belongs to the relative clause.

C.recipe: added word creates the error (comma splice)
C.why_wrong: “It was a dancer ...” is a main clause, and joining it to “The young king Pepi II, however, was preoccupied with something else” with only a comma is a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: A period would make “A dancer whom the king ... urged him to guard day and night” a sentence of its own, but it has no main verb, so it is a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: history (Harkhuf, Sixth Dynasty official, led expeditions to Yam; the young Pepi II wrote to him about the dancer he was bringing back and asked that he be guarded closely, checked many times a night; Harkhuf had the letter inscribed on his tomb at Qubbet el-Hawa, Aswan). Known facts. Band-7 checks: cue outside a 6-word window (the verb that makes the fragment look like a clause is 13 words past the blank); run 34 words; reasoning steps 3.
band7_moves: noun phrase after the colon carries a relative clause whose finite verb (urged) arrives 13 words after the blank, past an interrupting phrase, so the period and semicolon options look as if they open a clause
a comma plus it was a decoy (e9aee0d8 menu)

band7.why: Exact band-7 menu of e9aee0d8 (colon, semicolon, ", it was a", period) after the announcing phrase "something else"; the noun phrase carries a relative clause with a finite verb ("urged") 13 words on, so the semicolon and period options look like clause joins.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a specified item
items.passage: A rattleback, an oblong object whose curved underside is slightly misaligned with the distribution of its weight, spins smoothly in one direction, but when it is spun the other way, it soon displays a peculiar ______ rocking motion that gradually halts its rotation and then sets it spinning in reverse.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “it soon displays a peculiar habit” is a complete main clause, and the noun phrase that follows, “a rocking motion that gradually halts its rotation and then sets it spinning in reverse,” specifies what that habit is. A colon correctly introduces that specification.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “a rocking motion that gradually halts its rotation and then sets it spinning in reverse” is a noun phrase, not a clause.

B.why_wrong: A period would make “A rocking motion that gradually halts its rotation and then sets it spinning in reverse” a sentence of its own, but it has no main verb, so it is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: With no mark, the two noun phrases “a peculiar habit” and “a rocking motion ...” run together with nothing to show that the second explains the first.

items.notes: Subject: natural science, physics (the rattleback or celt: a spinning object whose curvature is misaligned with its mass distribution; spun in its preferred direction it turns smoothly, spun the other way it starts to rock, loses spin and reverses). Known physics, no names. Band-6 shape of c468db1c and c101fc44 (announcing word, then a noun phrase); menu of f30a478e (semicolon, period, no mark). One-sentence run of 50 words; the announcing clause “it soon displays a peculiar habit” follows “when it is spun the other way,” inside a longer sentence.

band7.why: Announcing word plus a noun phrase with a relative clause, menu of f30a478e; the announcing clause is short and the colon is the natural reading, so band 6 as planned.

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas, with a comma before a supplement inside the item
items.passage: Working in strikingly varied styles, the Bengali artist Gaganendranath Tagore (1867–1938) produced satirical ______ ink paintings of Himalayan landscapes, some reflecting his interest in Japanese brushwork; and fractured, prismatic scenes of rooms and staircases that critics have compared to European Cubism.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: cartoons; often aimed at Calcutta’s westernized elite,
cartoons often aimed at Calcutta’s westernized elite,
cartoons, often aimed at Calcutta’s westernized elite,
cartoons, often aimed at Calcutta’s westernized elite;
items.explanation: The sentence lists three kinds of work, and the later items contain commas (“landscapes, some reflecting ...” and “fractured, prismatic scenes”), so semicolons separate the items, as the semicolon after “brushwork” shows. The first item, “satirical cartoons, often aimed at Calcutta’s westernized elite,” sets off its supplement with a comma and must end with a semicolon.

A.recipe: series errors (semicolon in the wrong slot)
A.why_wrong: The semicolon after “cartoons” splits the first item from its own description, making “often aimed at Calcutta’s westernized elite” look like a separate item, and the comma that follows fails to separate the first item from the second.

B.recipe: series errors (comma where the series needs a semicolon)
B.why_wrong: A comma after “elite” cannot separate the first item from the second when the items are divided by semicolons, as the semicolon after “brushwork” shows.

C.why_wrong: The comma before “often” is right, but the comma after “elite” leaves the first two items divided by a comma while the second and third are divided by a semicolon.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Gaganendranath Tagore, 1867–1938, Bengali painter and cartoonist: satirical caricatures of Bengali society, ink-wash Himalayan landscapes influenced by Japanese technique, and Cubist-influenced interiors of the 1920s). Known facts. Band-7 checks: cue outside a 6-word window (the semicolon after brushwork); menu of db24ecc9 (comma version, semicolon key, semicolon in the wrong slot, no comma before the supplement); one-sentence run of 41 words, the context folded into an introductory phrase; reasoning steps 4.
band7_moves: blank in item 1; the revealing semicolon comes after item 2, 12 words past the blank
second rule inside the option (comma before the supplement often aimed at ...), as in db24ecc9
three long items whose commas would let a commas-only reading look tidy

band7.why: Menu of db24ecc9: blank in item 1, the deciding semicolon after "brushwork" about 15 words later, and a second rule inside the option (comma before the supplement "often aimed at ..."). The semicolon-in-the-wrong-slot option is tempting.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: comma plus “and” before a clause with two introductory elements
items.passage: About four thousand years ago, herders and farmers constructed stone villages along the sandstone cliffs of Dhar Tichitt, in present-day Mauritania. The largest of these settlements contained hundreds of walled ______ by around 2,300 years ago, as the region grew increasingly arid, most had been abandoned.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The largest of these settlements contained hundreds of walled compounds” and “by around 2,300 years ago, as the region grew increasingly arid, most had been abandoned” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: When “and” joins two long main clauses like these, it is conventional to put a comma before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the main clauses run together, a fused sentence.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (the Tichitt tradition, Mauritania: dry-stone villages along the Dhar Tichitt escarpment from about 4,000 years ago, some with hundreds of compounds, largely abandoned by about 2,300 years ago as the climate dried). Known facts, no names. Band-6 shape of 7ce4ee13 and 59094d87: clause 2 opens with two introductory elements before its subject (“by around 2,300 years ago, as the region grew increasingly arid, most”), so the conjunction-without-comma option looks fine at a glance. No band-7 version exists for this template.

band7.why: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 with two introductory elements opening clause 2.

items.subtype: No punctuation inside a compound object joined by “and”
items.passage: In 2010, researchers reported three species of tiny animals called loriciferans living in the L’Atalante basin, a pool of brine deep beneath the Mediterranean Sea. Few organisms survive there because of the brine’s extreme ______ and complete absence of oxygen, yet the loriciferans appear to complete their whole life cycle there.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The brine’s extreme salinity and complete absence of oxygen” is a compound object of the preposition “because of,” with its two parts joined by “and.” No punctuation is needed between the first part and “and.”

B.why_wrong: A comma before “and” would separate the two parts of a two-part compound, “extreme salinity” and “complete absence of oxygen,” which is not conventional.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but it would split the object of “because of” and leave “and complete absence of oxygen, yet the loriciferans appear ...” with no clear structure.

D.why_wrong: A colon cannot separate the two halves of a compound joined by “and”; it would also come in the middle of the phrase that follows “because of.”

items.notes: Subject: natural science (loriciferans in the L’Atalante deep hypersaline anoxic basin of the Mediterranean, reported in 2010 as the first animals known to live their whole lives without oxygen). Known facts, team unnamed. Band-6 shape of 6ea8c23f (3.3, regions / regions, / regions: / regions;): a two-part compound after a preposition, the comma before and the natural trap. No band-7 version exists for this template.

band7.why: S4_compound has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 (compound after "because of", comma before and as the trap).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: comma before “and,” second clause opens with an although-clause
items.passage: Turacos, fruit-eating birds of African forests and woodlands, show brilliant crimson flight feathers when they spread their wings. This color comes from turacin, a pigment that contains ______ although chemists have been analyzing turacin since the nineteenth century, they have never found it in any other group of birds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “This color comes from turacin, a pigment that contains copper” and “although chemists have been analyzing turacin since the nineteenth century, they have never found it in any other group of birds” are both main clauses (the second one’s subject and verb are “they have never found”). Two main clauses can be joined with a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, so “copper, and” is correct.

A.why_wrong: A coordinating conjunction joining two main clauses needs a comma before it; “copper and although chemists ...” leaves it out.

B.why_wrong: The comma makes the although-clause seem to finish the first sentence, but the main clause “they have never found it in any other group of birds” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together, a fused sentence.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (turacos, African birds whose red flight feathers are colored by turacin, a copper porphyrin first analyzed in 1869 and known only from turacos). Known facts, no names. Medium shape of 083a35dc (clause 2 opens with an introductory element after “and”); menu of 870ae7ec and 2.17.

items.subtype: Closing a comma pair around an appositive between subject and verb
items.passage: Kenji Mizoguchi’s 1953 film Ugetsu draws on a far older work. Ugetsu Monogatari (Tales of Moonlight and Rain), a collection of nine supernatural stories published in 1776 by Japanese writer Ueda ______ had itself adapted earlier Chinese ghost tales, relocating them to Japanese settings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The appositive “a collection of nine supernatural stories published in 1776 by Japanese writer Ueda Akinari” describes the subject, “Ugetsu Monogatari (Tales of Moonlight and Rain).” It opens with a comma after the parenthesis, so it must close with a comma before the verb, “had itself adapted.”

A.why_wrong: A semicolon would cut the subject “Ugetsu Monogatari” off from its verb “had itself adapted,” leaving neither side a complete clause.

B.why_wrong: The appositive opens with a comma, so it cannot close with a dash.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, the appositive opened by the comma after the parenthesis is never closed.

items.notes: Subject: literature and film (Ueda Akinari’s Ugetsu Monogatari, 1776, nine supernatural tales adapted largely from Chinese sources and set in Japan; Mizoguchi’s 1953 film Ugetsu combines two of them). Known facts. Medium shape of 7f48b098 (2.1): appositive between subject and verb, opening comma 13 words before the blank, nutrients-style menu with a dash and a semicolon.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a short introductory phrase
items.passage: The coiled, chambered shells of the ram’s horn squid wash up on beaches worldwide, yet the deep-sea cephalopod that produces them had seldom been observed ______ 2020, a remotely operated vehicle exploring waters near Australia’s Great Barrier Reef captured the first video of one in its natural habitat.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first sentence ends with “had seldom been observed alive.” The second sentence opens with the introductory phrase “In 2020,” followed by its subject, “a remotely operated vehicle,” and its verb, “captured.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: The comma joins the main clause “a remotely operated vehicle ... captured the first video” to the first main clause with only a comma, a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no mark, “alive in 2020” attaches the date to the first clause, and the main clause “a remotely operated vehicle ... captured ...” then follows with only a comma, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “And” does join the two main clauses, but when a coordinating conjunction joins two long main clauses like these, it is conventional to put a comma before it; “alive and in 2020” leaves the comma out.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (Spirula spirula, the ram’s horn squid: its shells are common on beaches, but the animal was not filmed alive in the wild until 2020, by the Schmidt Ocean Institute’s ROV SuBastian off the northern Great Barrier Reef). Known facts, no names. Medium shape and menu of 67667d72 (2.10, “earlier. In” / “earlier in”): two-word opener whose date reads at first as part of clause 1.

fixes: D why_wrong called the and-option a comma splice; it is a conjunction without a comma (the comma after 2020 belongs to the introductory phrase), rewritten

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: Shatter cones are cone-shaped fractures that form in rock when the shock wave from a meteorite impact passes through it. Because no other natural process generates the necessary pressures, geologists regard shatter cones as dependable evidence of an ancient ______ using them to identify locations whose craters have long since been erased by erosion.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The main clause “geologists regard shatter cones as dependable evidence of an ancient impact” is complete. The participial phrase “often using them to identify locations whose craters have long since been erased by erosion” describes the geologists, the subject of that clause, and a comma correctly separates such a trailing modifier from the clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “often using them to identify locations ...” has no subject and finite verb of its own.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “Often using them to identify locations whose craters have long since been erased by erosion” a sentence on its own, and it is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “an ancient impact often using them ...” reads as if the impact were using the shatter cones; the phrase describes the geologists, so a comma is needed to set it off.

items.notes: Subject: natural science, geology (shatter cones: striated conical fractures formed by impact shock waves at pressures no other natural process reaches, used to confirm eroded impact structures). Known facts, no names. Medium shape and menu of 8f6d6ae6 (2.4, “CE, making”) and ac5536c1 (2.26, “fungi, producing”): the participial phrase describes the subject, and the no-comma reading attaches it absurdly to the nearest noun.

fixes: passage: "locations whose craters erosion has long since erased" (garden path, reads "craters erosion" as one noun) to "locations whose craters have long since been erased by erosion"; explanation and C quote updated

items.subtype: Opening a dash pair around an appositive between subject and verb
items.passage: The khomus, a jaw harp of the Sakha people of Siberia, is traditionally forged by a blacksmith. Its slender steel ______ the flexible strip that the player plucks—vibrates as the musician reshapes the mouth to emphasize particular overtones.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The phrase “the flexible strip that the player plucks” explains what the tongue is and is supplementary: without it, the sentence still reads correctly, with the subject “Its slender steel tongue” followed by its verb. The phrase is closed by a dash before the verb “vibrates,” so it must also open with a dash after “tongue.”

A.why_wrong: The supplementary phrase closes with a dash before “vibrates,” so it cannot open with a comma; read as a single mark, that dash would also come between the subject and its verb.

B.why_wrong: With no mark, “tongue the flexible strip” runs the phrase into the noun it explains, and the dash before “vibrates” has no partner.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but it would cut the subject “Its slender steel tongue” off from its verb, “vibrates,” leaving neither side a complete clause.

items.notes: Subject: arts, music (the khomus, the Sakha iron jaw harp, made by smiths; the player plucks the steel tongue and shapes the mouth to select overtones). Known facts, no names; framed on construction and technique, away from the official Inferences item on Sakha songs about ecosystems. Medium shape of 7f226b4b (2.18): the blank opens the dash pair between subject and verb, and the partner dash follows 6 words later, right before the verb “vibrates,” so a comma-plus-lone-dash reading fails.

items.subtype: Comma after a long introductory participial phrase
items.passage: Between about 1000 and 1130 CE, Mimbres potters in present-day New Mexico decorated bowls with elaborate black-on-white geometric designs. Placed over the heads of the dead in graves beneath the floors of ______ many of these bowls had first been perforated with a small hole.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The participial phrase “Placed over the heads of the dead in graves beneath the floors of homes” introduces the main clause and describes its subject, “many of these bowls.” A comma correctly separates an introductory phrase from the main clause that follows it.

A.why_wrong: Without a comma, the 14-word introductory phrase runs straight into the subject “many of these bowls,” so the reader cannot tell where the main clause begins.

B.why_wrong: The period makes “Placed over the heads of the dead in graves beneath the floors of homes” a sentence on its own, and it is a fragment.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but the participial phrase before it has no subject or finite verb.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Classic Mimbres black-on-white bowls, about 1000 to 1130 CE, southwestern New Mexico, buried inverted over the heads of the dead under room floors and often “killed” with a punched hole). Known facts, no names. Medium shape of a427a52c (2.20): a long participial opener before the subject; menu of 5cc85f01 (2.25).

items.subtype: Semicolons between series items that contain commas
items.passage: Chinese writer Shen Fu’s memoir Six Records of a Floating Life (1809) originally had six chapters, but only four survive: one recalling his marriage to his wife, Chen Yun; one on leisurely pursuits, such as arranging flowers and growing miniature ______ one describing the hardships that drove the couple from home; and one recounting his travels.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists the four surviving chapters, and some items contain commas of their own (“his wife, Chen Yun” and “leisurely pursuits, such as ...”). The other items are already separated by semicolons, so a semicolon is also needed after “miniature trees” to separate the second item from the third.

B.why_wrong: Because the items contain commas, a comma after “trees” would blur where the second item ends; the list already uses semicolons between items, so it must use one here too.

C.why_wrong: A colon already introduces the list after “only four survive”; a second colon cannot separate two items within it.

D.why_wrong: With no mark, “growing miniature trees one describing the hardships” runs the second and third items together.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Shen Fu, Six Records of a Floating Life, written around 1809; of its six chapters only four survive: married life with Chen Yun, leisure such as flower arrangement and miniature trees, the misfortunes that saw the couple cast out of the family home, and travels). Known facts. Medium shape of c04e9136 (2.16): colon, then a three- or four-part series with internal commas, blank at the end of the second item.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: In 1973, archaeologists excavating a royal tomb in Gyeongju, South Korea, recovered a rare painting from the ancient Silla kingdom. On a saddle flap made ______ layered birch bark, an artist had depicted a white horse galloping through the clouds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Layered birch bark” is the object of the preposition “of” in the phrase “made of layered birch bark.” No punctuation belongs between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause; “On a saddle flap made of” is not one, and a colon cannot separate a preposition from its object.

C.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate the preposition “of” from its object, “layered birch bark.”

D.why_wrong: A dash cannot separate the preposition “of” from its object, “layered birch bark.”

items.notes: Subject: arts and archaeology (Cheonmachong, a Silla tomb in Gyeongju excavated in 1973, named for the painting of a white flying horse on a birch-bark saddle flap found inside). Known facts, no names. Easy shape and menu of a1e0c981 (1.5, “of”).

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: The Sarashina Diary (c. 1060) records the recollections of a Japanese noblewoman known only as the daughter of Sugawara no Takasue. She describes how, during a childhood spent in a remote province, she longed to ______ The Tale of Genji, a celebrated novel then circulating in handwritten chapters.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The Tale of Genji” is the object of the verb “read” in “she longed to read The Tale of Genji.” No punctuation belongs between a verb and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon cannot come between a verb and its object; “she longed to read” is not complete without the work she longed to read.

B.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate the verb “read” from its object, “The Tale of Genji.”

C.why_wrong: A dash cannot separate the verb “read” from its object, “The Tale of Genji.”

items.notes: Subject: literature (the Sarashina Diary, about 1060, by the daughter of Sugawara no Takasue, who recalls longing in the provinces to read The Tale of Genji and reading it day and night once an aunt gave her the chapters). Known facts. Easy shape and menu of 96499989 (1.15, verb and object).

items.subtype: Embedded question: statement order and a period
items.passage: Linguists use the term “eggcorn” for a mistaken version of a word or phrase that remains meaningful to its user, such as “egg corn” for “acorn.” Such substitutions can reveal how ______ An acorn, after all, is a seed shaped somewhat like an egg.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “How people reinterpret unfamiliar expressions” is an embedded question: it is the object of “can reveal” inside a statement. An embedded question keeps statement word order (“people reinterpret,” with no “do”), and because the whole sentence is a statement, it ends with a period.

A.why_wrong: The sentence is a statement, not a direct question, so the embedded question cannot use question word order (“do people reinterpret”) or end with a question mark.

B.why_wrong: An embedded question keeps statement word order; “how do people reinterpret” is the order of a direct question.

D.recipe: question errors (question mark on a statement)
D.why_wrong: The word order is right, but the sentence is a statement, so it should end with a period, not a question mark.

items.notes: Subject: language (eggcorns, reshaped words that still make sense to the user, named after “egg corn” for “acorn”; term coined on Language Log in 2003). Known facts, no names. Easy shape and menu of aab78b25 (1.7): embedded how-question ending one sentence, another sentence after it.

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: comma before “but”
items.passage: In a 1994 study, researchers posing as panhandlers asked strangers for spare change. Relatively few people gave money when the researchers requested a ______ more people gave when the request was for an unusual amount, such as 37 cents.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Relatively few people gave money when the researchers requested a quarter” and “more people gave when the request was for an unusual amount” are both main clauses. Two main clauses can be joined with a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, so “quarter, but” is correct.

B.why_wrong: A coordinating conjunction joining two main clauses needs a comma before it, and “quarter but” leaves it out.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses; “quarter, more people gave” is a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together, a fused sentence.

items.notes: Subject: social science, psychology (the “pique technique”: in a 1994 field study, requests for odd amounts such as 17 or 37 cents drew more compliance than requests for a quarter or any change). Known study, authors unnamed. Easy shape and menu of 155239cf (1.27, “time, but”).

items.subtype: Comma between items of a simple series
items.passage: In 1949, New Zealand economist Bill Phillips constructed the MONIAC, a machine of transparent tanks and pipes that used colored water to simulate a national economy. Water circulating through the machine represented money that households spent on ______ deposited as savings, or paid in taxes.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three things households do with money: “spent on goods,” “deposited as savings,” and “paid in taxes.” Items in a simple series are separated by commas, so a comma belongs after “goods.”

A.why_wrong: With no mark, “goods deposited as savings” runs the first and second items of the series together.

C.recipe: series errors (semicolon in a simple list)
C.why_wrong: A semicolon separates series items only when the items contain commas of their own; these do not, and the rest of the list uses commas.

D.why_wrong: A single dash cannot separate items in a series; the list already uses a comma between its other items.

items.notes: Subject: social science, economics (the MONIAC, the hydraulic model of the British economy that Bill Phillips built at the LSE in 1949, with water standing for money flows). Known facts. Easy shape and menu of 6fece68e (1.3): blank after the first of three items. Claimed before the FSS hydraulic-integrator item (claims.txt line order).

review.note: Concept overlap with FSS w5b3_19 is resolved: that item's water-integrator claim was WITHDRAWN in claims.txt; MONIAC kept.

items.subtype: No punctuation before a restrictive that-clause
items.passage: On July 16, 1945, scientists detonated the world’s first nuclear weapon at a remote test site in the New Mexico desert. The explosion’s intense heat melted the surrounding sand into a thin layer of greenish, slightly radioactive ______ became known as trinitite, after the test’s code name, Trinity.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “That became known as trinitite” is a restrictive clause: it identifies the glass and is needed for the sentence to make sense, and “that” is its subject. A restrictive clause is not set off by a comma, so “glass that” is correct.

A.why_wrong: Without “that,” the verb “became known” has no subject, and the comma does not supply one.

B.recipe: added word creates the error (word dropped)
B.why_wrong: Without “that,” “slightly radioactive glass became known as trinitite” leaves two main verbs, “melted” and “became,” in one clause with nothing to join them.

D.why_wrong: A clause beginning with “that” is restrictive and is not set off by a comma.

items.notes: Subject: history and science (trinitite, the green glass formed from desert sand by the Trinity test, July 16, 1945, New Mexico). Known facts, no names. Easy shape and menu of cabe71d4 (1.29, “company that” / “company,” / “company” / “company, that”).

items.subtype: Semicolon between independent clauses
items.passage: The serinette, a small hand-cranked barrel organ, was popular in eighteenth-century France among people who kept canaries. Owners used it to teach their pets fashionable ______ a bird heard the instrument’s high, flutelike notes repeatedly until it could imitate the melody.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Owners used it to teach their pets fashionable tunes” and “a bird heard the instrument’s high, flutelike notes repeatedly until it could imitate the melody” are both main clauses. A semicolon can join two main clauses without a conjunction.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the two main clauses; “tunes, a bird heard” is a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together, a fused sentence.

C.why_wrong: A coordinating conjunction joining two main clauses needs a comma before it, and “tunes and” leaves it out.

items.notes: Subject: arts, music and history (the serinette, an 18th-century French bird organ, a small barrel organ cranked by hand to teach caged canaries tunes). Known facts, no names. Easy shape and menu of 1724dac2 (1.4, “advance,” / “advance” / “advance;” / “advance and”).
